utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good afternoon to everyone. May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Joanna Korner and Crispian Smith for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic Eugene O'Sullivan, and Ms. Tatjana Savic appearing for Stanisic Defence this afternoon. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic and Aleksandar Aleksic appearing for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I don't know if you are about to raise what I was about to, that is, the motion for videolink, the videolink testimony of 008.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not. And also can I apologise for my slightly casual attitude outside court. I hadn't appreciated, when I was talking to the Legal Officers, that Your Honour was sitting there. So Your Honour may have heard some remarks which I would not have otherwise made, and I think I ought to say that in open court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I'm tempted, Ms. Korner, to let you remain under the illusion that I did hear something, and actually, as I took my seat you were leaving, so -- so you are relieved.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Ah. Well, I was somewhat appalled when I turned around to see that you were sitting there, if I can put it that way. May I say, it was nothing entirely disrespectful, Your Honour, to anybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I'm certain that it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, actually, there is the videolink motion, which -- if Your Honours want to deal with first. But I want to raise the exhumation database, which is the order was to file today. The revamping.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, so what is -- are you reporting on the progress on that, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, yes, I mean, unfortunately it's more than reporting on the progress, it's a plea and an application for one more day. It has turned out to be a major task. We've had something between 8 to 10 people working on it since the order was given, with - I hope you don't mind - Christmas day off and boxing day. But unfortunately one of the problems was that we needed permission to get access to the ICMP database in order to give the dates that we were asked to give for each of these documents. And we only got that permission yesterday. And so people have been working effectively around the clock. But in order to try and make it entirely accurate, and I underline the word "try," could we have one more day?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The Chamber will allow until Friday morning. I now recall that this was a matter that was dealt with just before Christmas, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It was, Your Honours. And then, in fact, we applied -- because of the change in the order, we applied to the Duty Judge for an extension of time which he gave us until today. And thank you very much for Friday morning. Then, Your Honours, you were about to deal with the videolink motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber has before it the motion from the Prosecution to receive the testimony of Witness 008 by videolink. I believe the dates -- the proposal is the 24th and 25th of January. And we would be appreciative if the Defence could respond, we hope, by the close of today.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, as far as Stanisic Defence is concerned, because I haven't consulted with my learned friend from Zupljanin Defence, I can -- I can state our position right away. If it pleases the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, understanding the situation and the circumstances, we do not oppose the motion. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: We do the same. So we have no objection to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. So -- so the order is as prayed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours. Can I say, if the witness was perfectly prepared to return, it was his medical condition which -- which made VWS suggest that this was not a good idea. Your Honours, finally, can I return to this witness. And in the light of my past record you won't be surprised at what I have to say. Doing the very best I can this morning and this afternoon, I've been trying to cut down on the documentation that he should look at, Mr. Brown, but it really is going to take me the rest of the afternoon to deal with his original report and at least a further hour, I think, on the Monday morning to deal with the Mladic aspect, and I -- and so I'm asking for the rest of this afternoon in chief and one further hour on Monday morning. I suppose the only thing I can say is he is the only military expert who's dealing with the military documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Doing the arithmetic, Ms. Korner, this doesn't -- having regard to the five hours that one side has asked for, I can't remember the --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Two and a half.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: -- two and a half, this wouldn't present a problem in terms of the witness returning to his other duties, would it?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. No, it wouldn't, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So -- and it stops me putting in a complaint about the late delivery of the Defence documents, which arrived 24 hours later than they should have. If I can have the extra time because then we won't get to cross-examination today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, of course we do not oppose the application of Ms. Korner, and it's true that we are delayed, but I already explained that the delay is caused because of the -- some technical difficulties which we had with the uploading of the documents and the whole mass of the documents which we were dealing with. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, we remember you alerted us to that on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Could we have the witness back on the stand, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, good afternoon to you, sir. Before Ms. Korner continues, I remind you you're still on your oath. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, yesterday, and perhaps we should deal with this first, Judge Harhoff asked you if you were in possession of any evidence to show that paramilitary groups were assigned particular tasks by the military, such as mopping up. And you said that you would want to refresh your memory overnight. And I wondered if you are able to help.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I necessarily saw specific instructions or direct orders to individual paramilitary units using the phrases "mopping up." In my report I do reference two paramilitary groups that I know were subordinated or integrated into the VRS. That being Milankovic's Group which I talked about yesterday which had acted as a volunteer unit in Western Slavonia and later was integrated into the VRS, I believe, and Milankovic himself was given a rank. And he was later sent to Knin, I believe, and died later in 1992. The second group that I reference in my report is a group from Prijedor, Cigo's Group. Which similarly was utilised in Western Slavonia and, I believe, in an open source document as a sort of sabotage group. Sometimes these groups are given names as intervention platoons, sabotage groups, and the like. Cigo's Group was used in Western Slavonia in 1991 and was part of the 43rd Motorised Brigade in Prijedor. And, again, in an open source reference purportedly written by Cigo himself, he was involved, as a 43rd Motorised Brigade was as well, was involved in operations in Prijedor in May and June and later in the summer, in 1992. There is also a document written by the Main Staff in July --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Hold on a minute, Mr. Brown. In both of the two cases that you have referred to and which we have seen in your report, you just refer to operations, and so my question would be, before you leave these groups, Are you aware of the kind of tasks that these groups performed in those operations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not in detail, sir. I clearly know that the 43rd Brigade was involved in operations in Prijedor, and I'm assuming that Cigo's Group was involved in that, in the attacks. But in terms of the details --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: In what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there was an attack on Prijedor and Hambarine, Kozarac in the late May 1992. This is reported by the 1st Krajina Corps in their documents, seizing control of the territory. There was a flash-point incident in Hambarine in which some JNA soldiers were attacked. After that there was a large military operation in Kozarac and Hambarine which involved the use of that brigade, amongst others. A large number of civilians were rounded up and sent to detention centres after that, obviously notably in Omarska and Keraterm and Trnopolje. And I'm assuming that Cigo, as part of that brigade, was also involved in that operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And you can't be more specific?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't be more specific on the role of Cigo within the 43rd Brigade, but I do know the 43rd Brigade was in involved in that operation and congratulated, by the way, by General Talic in an instruction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Back to you, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. In fact, Your Honour, we'll come to the section report that deals with it and have a quick look at the report on the paramilitaries.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, can I go back to where we left off yesterday. We were dealing, yesterday, with the area of responsibility of the corps and their cooperation with the civilian authorities. And if you take your report and if we go to paragraph 1.108, which in English is at page 46. There, you deal with the Crisis Staff relationship with the Crisis Staffs, in the plural, relationships with the military, and you set out there in fairly full detail, but we may as well have a look at the document, the Prijedor decision which was published in the gazette which -- could we -- it's footnote 154; it's tab 10 of the documents, and it is 466. And as we discovered yesterday, it's part of the law library. If we look very quickly at this, Article 2 of the document says that it's been -- "Prijedor Municipal Crisis Staff has been established to coordinate the functions of the authority, the Defence of the municipal territory," and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If we go to Article 6, please, next page in English and also in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff shall, in particular, coordinate the work and activities of all components of All People's Defence, consider mobilisation, deal with issues of supply requirements, and the like.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then finally, at Article 9, which is on the last page of the document. And it's the same page in B/C/S actually. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff shall, at all times, cooperate with the army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and so on and so forth. And I think that you note in your paragraph that although you saw documents where the Crisis Staff appeared to be actually giving instructions to the military, by and large it seems to have been a relationship of cooperation; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think there are similar documents in a number of other municipalities. Kljuc is one; Kotor Varos is another; Prijedor, obviously. And this coordination function not only seems to be articulated in this document but I would argue also occurred. I would also just note that there is a -- the collection of information in the municipalities is referenced in Article 12. So it's not just this coordination and leaving the municipality in isolation; there is also a reporting process. So the collection of information on -- in the municipality and reporting that through a chain. But I think Sanski Most was one most where they may have been slightly more forceful. And did I see one or two references where the military were instructed or given some more forceful instructions to do various issues. But this seems to be a common feature in a number of the municipalities that I have seen documents from.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. And we've already looked at the Kljuc document, which says much the same thing. Yes, thank you very much. You then -- continuing with your report. You point out that it would appear that lower-level officers, or lowish-level officers, who were, for example, brigade commanders became either members of the local Crisis Staff or ex-officio members; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I know in Prijedor, for example, Vladimir Arsic or Zeljaja were local commanders there. I've seen a document in Kotor Varos where Commander Bosko Peulic, who was the 122nd Brigade - actually, he was also OPS group Vlasic which is a wider zone, one of the zones I mentioned yesterday - he briefed or was present in some Crisis Staff meetings. I've also seen references, I believe, in Kljuc municipality where military commanders and not necessarily named commanders but military commanders were briefed or had been present.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then moving through, if we look, please, you dealt with and I think we touched on that yesterday, the relationship between the 1st Krajina Corps and the ARK regional Crisis Staff. And moving to paragraph 1.116, page 51, we see there that apparently relationships weren't very good because they wanted mandatory attendance, the ARK Crisis Staff, of General Talic or someone designated by him. And then in paragraph 117 -- 1.117, you note that reports dealing with the overall situation, the 1st Krajina Corps were under control. If we look, please, at the documents, please, that you reference, or two of the documents you reference, first one is at tab 21 and is 689. It's already -- I'm sorry, it's already an exhibit, Defence Exhibit 2D0001. All right. Dated the 8th of June, just to note that under "combat readiness" it states that the front line is stable throughout the zone and some units are continuing to mop up and search the areas of Prijedor and Kljuc. But then situation on the ground, the situation on the ground is under control, and the cooperation with the CJB, the public security centre, the police stations, and authorities has been fully established.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then if we look, please -- well, I suppose, yes, if we go over the page to paragraph 8 of this report.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: By the 8th of June, General Talic is reporting that we are fully controlling the territory and successfully holding our current positions. And then if we look, please, at the next document, which is a report a couple of weeks later, 23rd of June, at tab 25. The number is 3703. And if we look there, please, at paragraph 3, situation on the ground, sabotage keeps reoccurring, but throughout the entire territory of our area of responsibility, the organs of the civil authorities and the army have established control and prevent the activity of terrorists. From seeing those two documents, is that a theme that reoccurs, that there is control pretty quickly and that it's been exerted through cooperation of the police and the civil authorities?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think there were some sporadic incidents even after this date; for example, in Kotor Varos there were some operations not long after this 23rd of June, and there were some references through the documents into the summer of small groups that were being dealt with. But in terms of establishing control, the authorities and the military seemed to have established control very quickly, bearing in mind the army was established in the middle of May and here is, within weeks, there has clearly been operations prior to this in Prijedor, Sanski Most, Kljuc, and the likes, but they are stating in this, and the previous document, that they have got the situation under control, although I would say that there are still a small number of flash points that do occur around there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may that last document, 370 - what did I say it was? - 3, yes, could that be admitted and marked, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P1785, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You then carry on in the report for a number of paragraphs, and I want to move on to a further topic, to point out that although there were hiccups in this relationship between the military and the civilian, it -- that there were attempts to rectify problems which arose. And you deal with that in paragraph 1.122.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I wouldn't be under any illusion that it was - I think I used the phrase "seamless" in the report. It wasn't appear to be -- or didn't appear to be a seamless relationship at times. The military do make references to the need to establish better cooperation between the organs. So there are times when the relationship clearly would appear to be strained, but there are references that they are trying to improve that by holding meetings or discussions. But overall it would seem that they control the territory very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Then I don't want to go -- as I say, the report speaks for itself and you reference the documents. You then deal, at paragraph 1.127, page 55 through until the end of this section, with the removal of Muslims and Croats from the military. Again, I don't propose to highlight any particular part of it. You'd mentioned Colonel Hasotic and dealt with it in brief, and you referenced the documents. So can we move now, please, to the military operations section which starts at page 60 of the English. And you set out in the first few paragraphs what you call the general characteristics; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you state that the combat actions, in paragraph 2.2, undertaken by the corps can be divided into two distinct but overlapping categories. The first were a series of operations designed to seize control of and secure territory claimed by the Serbs and which would assist in the establishment of the borders of the Serbian state, and you say the second category of operation - this is paragraph 2.3 on the next page - consisted of large-scale, formal military operations. Now, we're going to look at it in a bit more detail, but can you perhaps outline to the Court what the essential differences were between these two kinds of combat actions; and secondly, whether the police -- or in what category the police would have been used?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are a number of notable differences. In relation to the first one, which is operations to secure control of territory, they tended to be at municipal level, using brigade, TO, and police units, often discussions in Crisis Staffs. They weren't necessarily linked, i.e., a brigade, one brigade, in this next municipality, although there sometimes was the movement of some units from one area into another municipality, but they seemed to be a little bit more localised, usually around a brigade or TO level. And they were over very quickly, generally, the operations. They were often categorised as operations to disarm the population or disarm groups. They often involved, for example, in Prijedor, and I believe in Kljuc as well, deadlines for the surrender of weapons, and then operations often joint or with the involvement of the police to take control of territory. And as I say, they generally were over very quickly, within a few days, although there might have been continual action over a week, a few weeks, later on, renegade groups. And they invariably involved the rounding up or taking into custody of numbers of prisoners. The second type of operation - and, really, I'm only referring to Operation Corridor and Operation Vrbas, for the corps - were very much longer in terms of time. They involved large numbers of troops, multiple brigades. And they were directed from -- with clear avenues and axes, from Main Staff directives. And, if you like, they were more akin to large military operations to seize -- in the case of the corridor, to seize the corridor area and link the 1st Krajina Corps with the East Bosna Corps. And in the case of the Vrbas operation, which was a smaller operation than the corridor operation, but to seize the territory around Jajce. In the second type of operation, I do know that there were police involvement, or there was police involvement, in Operation Corridor, albeit, you know, at a relatively small level, as a formed police unit. And there was also, I believe, an RSK/MUP unit, so a police contingent from the RSK were also involved. And that operation took some considerable time. It was relatively successful very quickly, although the operation continued through the summer and into the autumn, in order to expand the corridor. And they achieved the goal very quickly, but they continued to conduct operations to expand the corridor and take control all the way up to the river.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. All right. We're going to look at it in a little bit of detail, but can I just ask you this: The military unit that took part in the attack on Kozarac and Hambarine was, I think, was it, the 43rd Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah. Looking for a moment at issues of command and control, in order for that unit to have been involved in that attack, would the authority have lain with the commander of the unit, Colonel Arsic, or would he have had to seek permission from his superiors?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would imagine he had to seek permission from his superiors. It may not necessarily be, You are to attack this place at this time. It may be of something of a more general nature: You are to secure territory, or you are to establish control, or you are to ... so the actual, specific nature of the instruction may be more general. And it tends to be more general the further you go up, I have to say. But I know that General Talic was aware of the operation, and I know that he congratulated the operation and that he passed on the success of controlling Prijedor up to the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And from your overall reading of, I think, thousands of documents to do with this particular area and General Talic, can you give us some idea of what kind of commander General Talic was? In other words, was he somebody who was a hands-on or who would let his subordinates just carry on and do what they wanted?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I never met General Talic, and I can't tell you what he would be like as an individual. I can only --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm looking at --

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- explain from the documents. General Talic was someone who had been in operations for sometime. He had been serving in Croatia, he was a career JNA officer, and he had been involved in basically operations from late November 1991. And that continued all the way through till, well, the end of the Bosnian war in 1995; he remained the corps commander there. From what I see, he has a very effective and very functioning corps. The corps does not seem to check pace or stall when there is the transition between the VRS and the JNA, or the JNA and the VRS. There are still the same reports going up to his superior headquarters. And the detailed reports that his -- he and his staff produce are what I would expect to see in a very competent, functioning corps headquarters. And, as I say, the operations that he does conduct, his forces conduct quickly, and he is successful. For example, the operation in corridor, I think the instruction is given out in early June, and it's only within a matter of weeks that he's already pulled together all the forces, and they are rather significant, of his corps to go to that area to conduct the operation, and he's successful. So I think he's a good commander whose staff are aware of what is happening in his corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. And you said he certainly knew about, for example, the attack on Hambarine and Kozarac. Did he report that to the Main Staff of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did, in his regular combat reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And is that a feature that -- of his reporting, that he reports these kind of incidents and attacks to the VRS Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is. And it wasn't available to me at the time I wrote this report but I did see a reference, I believe - I can't remember where it is or the date - but I do remember seeing a reference in the Mladic diary, not long after Prijedor, that he mentions to Mladic, because it's in the diary, that Prijedor is now under control - I forget the exact wording and language. And I don't know if that's a telephone call or whether it's a brief in present, a personal briefing. But it would seem that that was known.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, we are going to deal with that. I think we'll see it's at the beginning -- in fact, the beginning of June sometime. All right. Can we just then, please, look at a few examples of matters you've dealt with in your report. If we go, please, to paragraph 2.4, you highlight there the common features of the -- what you call the municipality level operations. And you say that the -- after the issuance of deadlines for handing over of weapons and all personnel, the shelling, attacking, destruction of villages, cooperation with the TO and the police force -- and police units - sorry - and then the movement into camps. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think that is -- appears to be a common feature in a number the municipalities that I was able to get documentation on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You then discuss, between paragraphs 2.6 and 2.9, the responses to incidents and the roadblocks and the like. And I don't think I need to go into that in any further detail than you've dealt with in your report. Then you go, at page 64, paragraph 2.10, into the deadlines for the handing over of weapons. And I think it is worth looking at a couple of examples. In the Krajina area, it appears to begin really, effectively, with Defence Minister Subotic's declaration of an imminent threat of war in April. Then on the 4th of May, the National Defence counsel of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, which references that instruction, calls for the setting of a -- sets a deadline for surrender of weapons. And you've set that out. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think it seems to be a natural follow on, that they reference his document. And I'm assuming they take the phrase "take all necessary measures" they take that bit as being -- allowing them to set this deadline to have weapons -- surrender of weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And then you note, if we just summarise the next few paragraphs, what the ARK Crisis Staff did, the extension of deadlines, the CSB adopting it and saying, as you set out at the bottom of paragraph 2.15, that they will consistently carry out the decision on the disarming of paramilitary units. However, if we just look for a moment at two documents that you reference in paragraph 2.17 which shows, if you like, the convergence between the military and the CSB. Could we look first of all, please, at document which is already exhibited, P561. Which is at tab 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm terribly sorry, I just have one clarification, if we can have. 17:20. Ms. Korner, you said: "... what the ARK Crisis Staff did, the extension of deadlines, the CSB adopting it and saying ..." however the 2.15 basically, in my understanding, is quoting the decision of the ARK Crisis Staff, not the CSB.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You're quite right. Yes, I accept that correction. That's exactly what they're doing. In fact, it's another document where the CSB say they are going to carry it out.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Here we see, dated the 14th of May, the order from Stojan Zupljanin to the chiefs of all public security stations, and others, and also copying it, apparently, to the minister of the interior, the Ministry of the Interior, for information: "In keeping with the decision of the Autonomous Region of Bosnia and Krajina regarding the surrender of illegally owned weapons and ammunition, public security stations must undertake the following," and then it's effectively making plans for the surrender or seizure of these illegally owned weapons and providing for the results. And then if we look now, please, at the document which is at binder -- at divider 8, and it's 0 -- I'm sorry, 884 is the 65 ter number. The combat report of the following day, if we look at paragraph 3, it appears that the military has been made aware, the last three lines: "Since the deadline for handing over illegally owned weapons has expired, the Banja Luka Ministry of the Interior organs are making appropriate preparations to take away the weapons, and people fear possible inter-ethnic conflicts." Does that show a pretty close knowledge of what each organ, if you like, is doing?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, I think it's important enough for the corps to send that up to the -- its higher formation. So it's obviously of some importance to them, and they obviously are very aware of it. I might also just draw your attention to the line before that said: "There have been no armed conflicts in this territory, but the situation is extremely tense." There were some minor incidents, I believe in early May, but I think, you know, this is a tense time. Talic is saying there is no conflicts yet. But it's clear that they are aware of this deadline and they are aware that the police have issued this instruction.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may that be admitted and marked, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P1786, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You then reference, in the next paragraph, 2.18 of your report, that the Krajina Corps were issuing and acting on deadlines for handing over of weapons and carried out operations themselves. And you reference those; Sanski Most, Kljuc, Prnjavor, Kotor Varos. And then you give the example, in paragraph 2.19, of the Prijedor municipality, and I don't think we need to look particularly at any of the documentation there. Can we move, then, please, next to the cooperation with the Territorial Defence, which starts at paragraph 2.22. And I think to a large extent we can deal with that in summary form because I think you more or less dealt with that when we looked at the combat readiness report. The territorial units, and you deal with this at some length, in fact were, as it were, transposed within the VRS, the 1st Krajina Corps area, into light infantry units; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was expected from the 16th Assembly Session. And General Talic's documents also indicated that that was to happen. And eventually, although it took a little period, that the Territorial Defence units were invariably renamed light infantry brigades.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And as you point out in paragraph 2.33, on the 17th of June - that's in the middle - Talic proposed to the Main Staff the establishment of a formal command structure called the group of light brigades command, and the -- this command was formed from Banja Luka and commanded by somebody called Colonel Petar Spasojevic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there had been a Territorial Defence command in Banja Luka. And I think probably what General Talic did was just to utilise that TO, existing TO headquarters, and rename it Banja Luka whatever I've written here, the Banja Luka -- the brigade command, and it consisted actually of light brigades in and around the Banja Luka area, a number of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And if we go to paragraph 2.35, and there is just one document I'm going to ask you to look at there, you point out well if we look at the previous paragraph -- by April, when we looked at the combat readiness report, the 1st Krajina Corps had in fact formed 24 light infantry brigades, each of them averaging about 1200 troops; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you then give the areas. And in paragraph 2.35, you reference the Kotor Varos Light Infantry Brigade being actively involved in most of the military operations, together with others, including the MUP. And can we look, please, now at document which has got the number 10636, tab 34. Is this an order emanating from the light infantry brigade of Kotor Varos?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. There weren't too many of this type of documents that I saw in the collection that we had, because this is actually a subordinate formations order, in this case the Kotor Varos Light Brigade, down to one of its own subordinate formations, in this case I think it's the mortar platoon. So this is the mortar platoon's copy of the Kotor Varos Light Brigade's commander's order for operations around this period in Kotor Varos. I'm not sure why it was in the collection, but it's one of the -- one of the subordinate unit orders.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And if we go -- it says [indiscernible] set out the background. He says, I've decided to -- next page, 2 in English, and also in B/C/S -- and he said -- he sets out what is to happen. And then at 5, tasks for subordinate units, and then in we go to 5.2 which we will find on the third page in the English and B/C/S, the 2nd Infantry Company, and then goes on to explain what it's going to do. And then it says: "With part of your forces, be ready to prevent the flaring up of new trouble spots on the territory of the village of Ravna. Acting in concert with the forces of Kotor Varos SJB, organise checking of unknown individuals and foreigners entering the area." Now, from your examination of the documents, and looking at the overall picture of the municipality operations, what was the role of the police in these operations, in general terms?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, most of the documents I've looked at obviously are military documents, and the ones that I do see referencing police involvement do have this phrase of cooperate or coordinate with the police in the takeover or control of territory. There was obviously an involvement later on in relation to captured personnel, but the documents that I do see that reference it invariably discuss -- discuss coordinating with police or cooperating with police, that includes in the Crisis Staff decisions. There are a couple of references in this document to cooperating with the police, not just in the 2nd Company, but I think the Pioneer's Platoon and elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If we look at the next one, 5.3, we see that acting in concert with -- to the Pioneer's Platoon, acting in concert, again, with the forces of the Kotor Varos public security station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But, Mr. Brown, what does this mean, in practical terms, to coordinate with the police? Thank you very much. I mean, it's completely open. Could be anything. What does it mean? In practical terms.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Invariably these orders are not written in isolation. There's usually some kind of discussion that goes with it. Coordinating with the police could involve the tasks that the police have been set in any previous discussion or to be -- to -- or to be implemented by the police, there is to be some coordination. For example, one of the tasks may be to the establishment of check-points. The police may be setting up check-points to secure an area or a road, prior to the attack, using military forces. There may need to be coordination in when that check-point is established, what its tasks are to be, issues of opening fire and coordinating fire, coordinating when the attack is going to happen and when it's expected to finish. So these documents are not -- you know, it's not in isolation. I would imagine there was probably a significant amount of planning that goes into this, and representatives, I would imagine, of neighbouring units as well, not just the police. I think it talks about neighbours. There's a planning component to this, and I would imagine cooperation means the police will have set tasks which will be agreed, the individual will be informed about the nature of this operation, how long it's meant to last. If, for example, there is to be the processing of prisoners, there has to be a coordination of effort in that. And so I would imagine that's -- that type of activity is what they are talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... if we go to -- sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And how about the legal structure. Were the police officers subordinated to the military, or was it just, as it says here, a mere coordination?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would have expected, if there was a direct subordination of police into this light infantry brigade for the conduct of this operation, I would have expected it to be quite specific and explicit in this document. And in the same way that the commander of this brigade outlines the exact tasks for his companies, the Pioneer Platoon, the mortar platoon, the intelligence section, if the police were directly subordinated to him, I would have expected an instruction in there that made it clear about what their tasks were to be, not the more general instruction here that seems to say, we are -- you are to ensure you coordinate with the police. If there was a direct subordination, I would have expected one of the paragraphs to read something along the lines of, "Such and such a MUP force is to do the following." But I don't see that in this document. And that would lead me to the impression that the subordination of the police in this operation is not one that the commander directly controls him but there was a police involvement in this operation which requires coordination and which the commander is aware of. And the police clearly are playing a part; I don't know what that part necessarily is from this document, but they are engaged in the operation. But from this, if it had been a direct subordinate, if he was -- the police, to all intents and purposes, were another unit within his brigade that he could task and command, I would have expected in one of those paragraphs for it to be explicitly stated there, and I don't see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I mean, the picture that you are proposing does seem to become a bit blurred. We spoke yesterday about how the volunteer groups and the paramilitary units were circling around more or less on their own, perhaps with some degree of coordination. And now we also have the police apparently not being directly subordinated to the military but just being required to be ready to undertake some tasks according to the local conditions but nothing more than that really. What is your assessment from a military point of view of these conditions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not see that as being an unusual circumstance, sir. And I can give you examples from my own military service where I've worked with policemen and I have worked in joint operations with policemen but I have not commanded them. When I was a very junior officer serving in Ireland in counter-terrorist tasks, I would routinely have policemen with me. We would have coordination meetings in relation to the tasks that we were set, they would be -- we would be conducting operations with them. But they weren't subordinated to me, they were subordinated to their police chain. And there was agreement about the tasks that they had, and there was agreements that I had. So it's not necessarily something I see as unusual.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Well, I'm not suggesting that it is unusual. What the Chamber is trying to do is to get a full picture of how this actually happened in practice. And so there must have been some sort of superior planning or, as you say yourself, agreements on exactly what role each of the participating units would have and who was controlling these activities. So if your answer is that it wasn't the military commander who controlled directly the activities of the involved police units, then it must have been the MUP somehow that instructed its units to do this and that on behalf of the military or with the police -- with the coordination of the army.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can only --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: How did it work out in practice; do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I can only assume that that is what happened. Because as I said before, if it wasn't that, if it was that the military in essence commanded and the police were directly subordinated, I would expect to see a lot of -- not just in this document, but a lot of other references. And I would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I have understood that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And I would expect what happened in practice, if you look at the Crisis Staff decisions, was that that was a group whereby agreement was made about territory to be controlled or operations to be mounted, and it may well have been that that was the forum at the local level where individuals would say, An operation is going to be conducted here, and the involvement in the police will be A, B and C; or we will be able to provide A, B and C support in the following way. And the military would be saying, Well, we are going to be conducting the operation and this is our part of it. I think that is one of the -- at the local levels, that is where these decisions seem to occur. And the Crisis Staff -- for example, if you look at the Kljuc municipality, they are meeting every day with military, police, and civilian leadership figures, talking about what has happened in the past and what is going to happen in the next day. And I think this is a very critical component of exactly how it was decided about what areas were going to be taken under control next.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Would the military in Kljuc be subordinated to the decisions made by the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think the Crisis Staff had this coordinating function. Clearly there was a military chain of command, and it is -- it is General Talic, it's his soldiers that are involved in that. But in Talic saying to his subordinates, You are to secure control of territory, you are to cooperate with the municipal authorities, you are to establish the closest links with the municipal authorities, I think his military commanders are then carrying out that instruction for him through the mechanism of the Crisis Staff and other localised meetings in order to secure that territory. And that gives them the legitimacy to have these operations through their own -- clearly the military have a chain of command, and the military brigade commanders will be issuing orders to their individual brigades, but this cooperative element to me seems to be very present. I don't see this subordination issue of, it's only the military in command and anybody else who's involved is under that -- I don't see that. I would expect to see other indicators there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- nor from my own military experience do I -- would I necessarily find it unusual.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Can we just, for a moment, then, dealing with what you told Judge Harhoff about your experience in Northern Ireland, look at this part. You said that when you did joint operations, there was a -- you dealt with the military, and the police had their own -- I think I better just get your own -- I'm sorry. I'm summarising rather badly what you said. I'll go back to what you said. Yes. You would have coordination meetings in respect of the tasks, but they were not subordinated to you, they were subordinated to their police chain. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, there can be different -- different instructions given. Police can be subordinated in certain circumstances to the military, but there has to be certain criteria met. But in my experience that didn't happen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I just want to move one step further on that, as you -- as it's been brought up now. In the event that there is a joint police/military operation going on, first of all, have you seen any indication in any of the documents you've looked at that the military would be the people to deal with any disciplinary or criminal infractions that were committed by the police during the course of a joint operation?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe if I could step back first, talking about the documents of subordination, if we're talking about that now, there were a couple of documents in which, if the military wanted to have police subordinated to them in combat operations, there would have had to be agreement between the corps and the CSB or SJB, that -- there are a number of documents I think two or three.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We will look at them.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I know that there was one document which that did happen, in November, where there was a request and it -- and it happened. So as I said, there can be mechanisms where police can be subordinated. And in my own -- even in my own previous military service that could happen. It didn't happen to me. When we worked with operations with the police, there was an agreement in what the police were there to do and the tasks that they were there to do, but I did not -- I did not -- they were not a subordinate unit from me. In relation to discipline -- sorry, your question was related to discipline.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Disciplinary, yes. First of all, simply arising because we're dealing with it at this stage, in respect of the VRS documents that you looked at and in -- specifically in relation to the 1st Krajina Corps, did you see any evidence in those documents of the military dealing with infractions, whether disciplinary or criminal offences, committed by the police, in other words going through the military disciplinary proceedings rather than the police?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In your own personal military experience, if there was a joint operation going on and the police committed a disciplinary offence during the course of that operation, who would deal with that, the police or the military chain of command?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my experience, the -- it would be the police commander, I mean, I, as a grand commander, would be expected to make a report to my superior command about an incident, but it would not be the responsibility of my superior commander to charge a policeman. My commander would be expected to pass on the details of that to the policemen's chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't my commander or I or anyone else may be held accountable for not doing that and not passing that on, but I was not in a position -- I was a junior officer, I have to say, but I know my commanding officer would not have the power to charge a policeman in my -- in my experience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Even if that policeman was under your authority?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If he had been -- if there had been agreement and direct subordination had been agreed, and there are mechanisms at the extreme end when policemen can be placed under the command of military personnel, and he was subject to the army law, I would suspect he probably could, although I'm not a legal expert, I'm not a lawyer. But from my experience and the operations that I did, if a policeman had conducted himself in a manner that required some disciplinary process, I was expected to report that through my chain of command. But it was not, I believe, my commander's responsibility to charge him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can we conclude with the document that we were looking at. If we go to paragraph 11. And I think that reinforce -- you may see that reinforces the point you make; there's no direct order there.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, is it paragraph 11 of the --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Eleven of the same document we're looking at, at 34.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I think there's a reference to neighbours; that probably means neighbouring units.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Yeah, if we look at that, it says, For security support, in all units be ready with part of your forces to break up and destroy infiltrated sabotage terrorist groups and other enemy special forces acting in concert with neighbours and the police forces on the ground.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then, Take prisoners of war to the brigade command where they would be interrogated and then to a prison camp. And we will come to that later.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm just checking whether this is an exhibit; no it's not. Could that be exhibited and marked, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P1787, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, could I -- I'm not quite clear, because of when we started, what time the break is going to be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, I think we could push it to the normal time of 5.20.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 5.20. Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, so can I now move, then, because it's the only document from that set, to your section where you actually go into some detail on the cooperation between the military and the police, which starts at paragraph 2.39 on page 75. Now, you point out that it was, in fact, a significant feature in many of the combat actions that took place in the Krajina during 1992, and you further point out that General Talic and Stojan Zupljanin were two of the most prominent figures because of their positions; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it would seem so.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then you list a number of different, as it were, requests, instructions, and information that went between them. And perhaps we can just look at a couple of examples of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we have a look, please, at document 3705, tab 27.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And there is a request or a document of 30th of June addressed to the Main Staff, which says that the CSB has approached the army with a request for 200 pieces of 7.62 millimetre or M-56 automatic rifles, and they are recommending that it be issued, particularly as the units are less interested in them apparently.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And, yes, I'm not sure [indiscernible] -- Your Honours, could that be exhibited and marked, please. Admitted and marked, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1788, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then, later on, this appears to have been a request, is that right, simply for arming police as police, as opposed to anything to do with military?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It would seem to be that maybe the police have just made a request, bearing in mind the size of the corps and maybe the equipment that they had, that they need to be armed, maybe in the conduct of their duties.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Much later on, it appears that there was a more formalised meeting or request. If we look, please, at document number 56, which is -- it's already been exhibited. Yes, P1668. This is dated the 21st of November, 1992, from General Talic to Zupljanin or his assistant, and, is this right, he's asking for police units with the strength of at least two battalions, and more if possible?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think, reading the document, there is obviously -- as I said, the operations in the corridor, although they were successful they wanted -- it continued, actually, through the year. And obviously, I think, in this case he's requesting for additional support for operations in that area, and he's making a request to the CSB for this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Does the word "request" have any significance in the sense of the relationship between the army and the CSB?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I just read the document quickly?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm reminded this document was put in under seal, so it ought not to go out on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He's -- having quickly read it, I don't think he's ordering Mr. Zupljanin, he's asking him for the help. He asks, well, quite forcefully, I think, and he's obviously got a requirement that the corridor maybe is threatened and that obviously that that was a very important area, but he's not ordering him, he's making a request or a -- or he's asking him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. We'll see later -- sorry, I was just listening. I've got the B/C/S on so I try not to talk over the English. We'll see later that there is an earlier document in July where General Talic appears to give an order to the police. What does that suggest about the relationship between the police and the army, or Talic and Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which instruction is that, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right, well, we'll look at it. It's -- I think you reference it in your report.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Jump ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours, I jumped ahead of myself and now I'm --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. If you look at paragraph 2.50.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You refer to a document which regrettably is not on our 65 ter list and so is not in, but -- on the 1st of July he passed an order to units of the corps noting that with the aim of improving the organisation and conduct of operations during combat activities, all police forces were to be placed under the command of the local military commander who shall be -- decide how they are to be used.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was the only reference I could see in the military documents about the placing of police under the command. There were the two documents prior to this which made reference, I think it's on the 19th of May -- there were earlier documents saying that if there was -- if the police were to be used or the military wanted to use the police, there had to be an agreement, had to be a request to the CSB. This document is the only one that I ever saw -- or this reference, actually, is the only one I ever saw with that explicit language. And I don't believe that this seemed to have occurred because, well, this document you've just referenced, the one in September -- or, sorry, the one in November.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: November.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's making a request again. He's not saying the police are mine and I can use them as I want. I'm not sure why he put this single reference in on that day. It could have been because of the activities of the CSB special unit in Kotor Varos which occurred around that period and which became known about and maybe it was a response to that. But even -- even with that instruction - and it is a slightly ambiguous line, I think, in the document - I did not see commands having police units under their -- under their command and them deciding how it's going -- they are going to be used after this instruction which is in July sometime.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, in fact I think we can see, if we look, please, at the next document, which was a Defence document. It's at tab 57. 2D00119. We see there the document from the CSB which says, at paragraph 1: "In accordance with the order from the Minister of the Interior of the Republika Srpska and on the basis of the dispatch from the commander of the 1st Krajina Corps, Strictly Confidential 709192," which is what that one was, the previous document, "and the consent of the Ministry of the Interior, set up a brigade." So ...

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it would seem that he accepted the request and it was -- it was implemented.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's probably, then, an appropriate moment for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. So we rise, to resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: While we wait for the witness to take the stand, it has been brought to my attention that the order that the Chamber made in respect of the application to receive the evidence by videolink didn't fully appear on the transcript. And while it isn't necessary for the Registry's purpose for us to formally issue a written decision, it is apparently necessary for me to repeat that the order has been granted as prayed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And also, before the witness is being brought back to the stand, the Chamber has a request to make to the Prosecution in respect of the motion for admission of evidence of ST-020 pursuant to Rule 92 quater. And the issue is that in the motion, the Prosecution added two annexes, two medical declarations, one of which was filed only in B/C/S and the other only in the English translation, without the B/C/S original. And the request that the Chamber would wish to make to the Prosecution is that if those documents are available in the other language, so to say, then could the Prosecution please provide them to the Chamber immediately.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, we were looking at the general issue, as discussed in your report, of cooperation between the military and police. And if we look at paragraph 2.41 of your report, you reference some documents where there are examples of that cooperation. And I think we can just look at those, please. The first is the document at -- which is P432.13 at tab 14. This is 29th of May regular combat report to the Main Staff. And we see, at paragraph 2, combat disposition of the units: "Units of the 1st Krajina Corps are holding positions taken earlier, and the front line has not moved. Cooperation with the MUP in mopping up the terrain and confiscating weapons from illegal formations in the area of Prijedor, Sanski Most, and Kljuc continues." An, again, going back to the questions Judge Harhoff --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, there appears that two terms are used for the -- for the one word in Serbian. In all the cases in these reports and the reports that we saw before, the word is -- in Serbian, is "sadejstvo" and it is -- it is translated sometimes as "acting in concert" and sometimes, as Ms. Korner just rightly said now, "coordination." Now, maybe in order that we have -- this is one of the important issues, I believe, in this case, and maybe with the help of the interpreters can we really opt for one interpretation in English of the -- of the word, in Serbian, "sadejstvo"? That is my suggestion in order that we have a clear situation further on in the case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, if I look at the B/C/S version in paragraph 2, it's -- which word do you say is the "cooperation"? Because it -- it doesn't -- cooperation is the first word in the English translation, which is not the word I think you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The word "sadejstvo" is the second word -- or the third word in the second --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: -- in the sentence of this, under 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, then what's the first -- actually, I can't ask you this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The first sentence is -- it is continued -- "continuance of the coordination" or "continuance of acting in concert."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, this is all a bit difficult, and the trouble is it's -- we've been going through this for -- now for nearly 18 months, I think, without this issue being arisen. I'm not sure whether the interpreters can resolve the issue for us. I mean, why -- do the interpreters in the booth, are they any better than the interpreters in CLSS or whoever did these documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I wasn't really --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Is the issue such that it can be determined once and for all?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I believe it is, Your Honours. Just that we use -- because the Serbian word is one word, and it's used throughout. The whole -- every each and every document has the very same word, and this is -- this is specifically a military term, and it has its explanation in Serbian language. Therefore, my suggestion is that we use only one term in English, corresponding to the fact that it's one term in Serbian. Whichever -- I'm not insisting whichever -- whichever word or words in English would be appropriate, I'm asking for help. And in order that we clarify the situation, that it is this precise Serbian word that is used, when we used, for example, "acting in concert," it means "sadejstvo," because "coordination" is the other word and can be used for some other purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I understand. But my question to you was really whether the Serbian word, even if the word is the same but used in a different context, would have a different meaning. So my question to you was: Is the Serbian word of such a nature that it can only be correctly translated with one, and only one, English word that then would have to be applied every time from now on?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, as far as my knowledge goes, this is a very specific military term. And usually it is used only in the military documents to explain a certain action of the -- of the military units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: May I suggest, Mr. Zecevic, that you put a request to CLSS to have this issue settled once and for all. Meaning that when this issue is used in a military context, what is then the correct English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I will, Your Honours. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Mr. Brown, what I was asking you about this document was, in the light of Judge Harhoff's requests, whether it's -- is any light shone on the role of the police by this, as to what they were doing?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I take it at face value what the document says, that they have conducted operations in cooperation with the police. If -- it doesn't say police units under my command have conducted A, B and C, or subordinated units to the 43rd Brigade have done A, B ... it says they have been working in cooperation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe I'll also draw your attention, if I can, to the -- reinforcing the issue that the territory was controlled quite quickly in paragraph 1, bearing in mind this is the 29th of May, so I think the attacks in Prijedor were the previous day or even the day before that, 27th. There are some weak resistance to confiscation of weapons in the wider area of Prijedor, Sanski Most, and Kljuc. The armed formations have been broken up, but some components from individual squads are still resisting. So ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, the -- Mr. Brown, you've got a remarkable recall, but the attack on Prijedor took place, in fact, the day after this, on the 30th of May.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, was that -- okay. Well, I think there was some activity prior to that, though, wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. All right. And then the other document I'd like us to look at, please - I think that one is an exhibit, isn't it, yes - is the document at tab 21, which is -- 2D001 -- we did. I think we've already looked at that, so I'm not sure we need to look at that one again. Yes. It just says -- yes, the cooperation [indiscernible]. All right. You then, again, pick the example of Prijedor as a demonstration, if we look at paragraph 2.43, of the cooperation that took place. And it's worth having a look at this for a number of themes, I think. The document is P672, tab 45. This is the report that was, in fact, supplied -- it was the commission investigating the so-called reception centres but it mentions other things, and if we look at the last page, it's dated the 18th of August. If we look at the last page.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, all right. I was waiting for it to come up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we have a look, please -- no. Sorry. It's not the same. I'm looking at a different -- sorry, yes, I see there seems to be -- I think it's --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm so sorry, Your Honour, I've got the same document in both, at 45 and 46, but they are supposed to be different documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: They are different documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: 46 is the --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 45. It's the CSB Banja Luka report.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Which is Exhibit P602. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Hopefully we now have the right one. Yes. And that's the commission.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we go -- rather than worrying about when the date is, could we go, on this point, first of all, to page 5 in English and page 7 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, this is the role of Prijedor SJB. And if we look at the second paragraph, it says: "After the outbreak of the armed conflict, at the request of the army, and as a result of the situation they found themselves in, employees of Prijedor SJB took part directly in the armed conflicts, during which 11 employees lost their lives. "Together with members of military units, employees of the police are searching the field, mopping up the remaining covert groups according to plan and under the direct command of the appropriate senior officers. At the same time, they are gathering operative information about the work of the adversary, bringing in persons, et cetera, suspected of armed rebellion," and then, again, "in collaboration with members of the military police, working in joint patrols, mixed check-points," et cetera, et cetera. Now as a description of what the police were doing, Mr. Brown, is this one that is a recurring description?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I think it would seem to echo what -- the earlier document you showed from Talic about operations in Prijedor as a cooperative component here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Now, simply because I don't want to go back to this document, can we go back to the previous page in English, page 4, and in -- it's page 6 in -- yes, page 6 in B/C/S, the resettlement of citizens. We see that according to the operational findings of SJB Prijedor, about 4 to 5.000 persons mainly of Muslim ethnicity left the municipality before the armed conflict. And then in the next paragraph: From the beginning of the armed conflict, in the municipality of Prijedor, until the 16th of August, 1992, according to data that have been insufficiently checked out, about 20.000 people, citizens, left the municipality, mainly of Muslim and Croatian but also of Serbian ethnicity. And I think you reference that part later on when you're dealing with the evidence of the, as it were, the removal of the non-Serb population; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe. I don't know if I referenced that specific quote, but probably this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I think we'll find you do. And then -- and the same -- on that same aspect, if we go forward again, please, to page 7 in English, the resettlement of citizens from Sanski Most, and that is on page 10 in B/C/S. Again, the report shows that about 3.000 persons have moved away from the municipality since the beginning of the armed conflicts. And up to the 16th of August, about 12.000 had applied, mainly of Muslim but partially of Croatian ethnicity, applied to Sanski Most to unregister. All right. Then, staying with your paragraph 2.45, you also reference the document - I hope this is the right document - which is P689; it's your footnote. And it's at tab 61. And if we go to page 4 very quickly, there we can see that you've already pointed out the military involvement in these operations in Prijedor. Here we can see confirmed that the combat operations which they say commenced on the 22nd of May employees of this station actively participated in these operations, primarily members of both active and reserve forces of the police; combat activities were at their most intense in the areas of Kozarac, and so on and so forth. And we can see that. And I think that's -- you then deal with Sanski Most in your -- sorry, in your report, going back to 2.45, and in -- yes, and also you make the point at the end of that paragraph that they were assisting in the establishment of the detention centres, took over the security of these centres from the army, and carried out interrogations and processing of prisoners. And you reference one of a number of those documents. And I'm just wondering if it's worth having a look at 2.47. No, I don't think it is. Then can we deal, can we move to where you do deal with the resubordination, which is at paragraph 2.49. You say -- and, again, we come to the question of what this word is, but for the most part the operations involving the police and the military were carried out in cooperation with each other; there were occasions when police units were directly integrated or subordinated to the VRS. You make the point there that there are fewer examples of direct integration of police units than for cooperative or joint operations, but you then give some examples of where that happened. And then in paragraph -- sorry, can I -- yes, I see, yes, can we have -- in the next paragraph you then give some examples of the correspondence between the army and the police about this, and I think we ought to look at that. Can we start with the document which is P376, at tab 12. Now, this is quite early on, 28th of May, and it's a document issued by Stojan Zupljanin to all SJBs - and this appears to be the one that went to Prijedor - the corps command, and the chief of corps security. And it talks about the activity, armed conflicts and military activity have spread. And then in paragraph 2: With regard to this matter and bearing in mind the fact that further uncontrolled activity could have major undesirable consequences, et cetera, all armed action and police activity is hereby forbidden without a prior decision and consent of this CSB and the relevant corps command of the armed forces of the Serbian Republic. From your study of the documents, were you able to see, Mr. Brown, why this order was issued?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know specifically why -- why it was -- why the police have issued this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say from my -- the military documents particularly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And then if we look --

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see those documents, by the way, as a -- when we're talking about the issue of subordination, I don't necessarily read it in relation to that. I read this more along the lines of both the police and the military wanting to ensure control of their units when combat actions are occurring so that in order -- I mean, it talks about coordinated and organised activity. They want to ensure that operations are coordinated, and I think what they are saying is if there is units doing -- you know, conducting operations on their own or firing of -- it can cause problems in coordinating their general structure. So I don't necessarily see this as a subordination issue, subordinating police; I see it as a control issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Well, on that note, let's look at the next document, please, that you reference, which is 65 ter 3704, at tab 24. This is approximately three weeks later, 19th of June, order on the use of the police in armed combat operation, signed by General Talic: "Since there are various ways of using the police force in armed combat operations, I issue the following. In the zone of responsibility, the police carry out tasks falling under the competence of the Ministry of the Interior and they are fully responsible for maintaining the law and order, preventing crime, and ensuring the successful functioning of units on the front. "The police may be used in direct combat operations on the front only exceptionally when it is necessary to hold and strengthen the front until the arrival of military units. In other cases, it's necessary to inform the chief of security services centre and receive his approval." So what was General Talic, as far as you can ascertain from your knowledge, dealing with here?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
