utterances.text: Well, I think he's saying that there are exceptional circumstances where the police can be used in combat operations. I would read this potentially from -- in -- through the optics of the corridor operations and, if you like, front lines where soldiers are holding positions. And maybe more akin to what happened in that instruction you showed earlier where a battalion was asked to be formed and raised in order to stabilise the front or hold the front. And if there is that requirement, then the CSB has to approve that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. So here they are saying the police can carry out tasks falling under the competence of the Minister of the Interior. General Talic appears to be drawing a distinction between the police tasks and the military tasks here?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he would seem to -- I mean, that would seem reasonable, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, may that be admitted and marked, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1789, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then other similar documents or documents that -- dealt with that one. Document number 40, I've already dealt with the two from November. Yes. And then I think you reference there, as I said earlier, the 1st of July instruction, and that's the end of paragraph 2.50.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think I dealt with that one.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We dealt with that one, yeah. Then again, summarising, as quickly as we can, the remainder of this report, I think you also showed that there was cooperation -- on the remainder of this part of the report, in the processing of prisoners, transfer between detention facilities. And we ought to look, perhaps, at one more document, and that is document at tab 52, which is P1094. This is rather like, I think, the last document that -- or the one before the last that we looked at. This is on the 18th of September, from Stojan Zupljanin, addressed to all SJBs and, again, to the command of the 1st Krajina Corps, the 2nd Krajina Corps. And it talks in paragraph -- the last paragraph on the first page in English, and I think it's over the page in B/C/S, if we go to the next page in B/C/S: At the same time, we draw to the attention of the SJB chiefs the fact that members of the active and reserve police forces may be engaged in combat activities according to the principle of resubordination to a superior army command only in the event that combat activities are taking place on the territory covered by the designated SJBs and with the approval of the chief of the CSB. Again, anything to show why Zupljanin was writing this in September? It's similar to the one he wrote way back in June.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would only speculate that the requests for combat operations in the corridor, that the police were trying to minimise that type of activity and that there had been these requests to send formed police units or units up to the front line, and maybe they felt that really was an army task that they shouldn't be conducting, that there was enough work in their own municipalities, as highlighted in one of the middle paragraphs, and that he was saying that really we should only be involved in combat operations if it's in our own area.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: And maybe it was to do with not wanting to release policemen up to the -- up to the front line to, in essence, act as soldiers in defending the corridor.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Yes. All right. And as I said, I don't think I need to draw the Court's attention to any other documents within this section. Can we turn briefly to paramilitaries because we have dealt quite a lot with that in your previous answers. Starting at paragraph 2.57 of your report. And as you've already, I think, explained to the Court, the involvement of paramilitaries was a complex one. I think that's the second sentence in paragraph 2.57. And let us look at the report you've already referred to in your answers to Judge Harhoff. The document is already an exhibit, and it's P591, tab 36. This report was produced by, as he was then, Colonel Tolimir; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In August of, as we can see, well, it's dated the 28th of July, but if one looks at the end, it appears to have gone out on the 13th of August. And he gives a long preamble as to what the characteristics of paramilitaries are. And then if we go, please, to the fourth page in English and the same in the B/C/S, he is listing some of the groups. And if we look at the fourth one on that page, there is a group with 13 members, headed by somebody called Zeljko Skrbic, which is active, and it says, on the instructions of somebody from the Jajce SJB, the said group armed and equipped itself with state-of-the-art supplies from a second engine fuel depot, then they turned outlaws, attempt to eliminate the command staff of the depot and take it over. To avoid punishment, Skrbic formally joined the 30th Krajina Division. Now, how does this fit in with your survey of the 1st Krajina Corps dealings with paramilitary organisations?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think this document, and others, indicated that they wanted to ensure that these units were brought under control and to be -- they were to be placed under the control of the army, and this would seem to be an example that they were, or at least this unit was anyway. But it seemed to be more that the issue of paramilitaries -- I mean, that they were -- there was a clear awareness. This is quite a detailed document. There was an awareness of what the paramilitaries were doing and also how many were with operating and some of the groups that were there, but that really -- instead of -- instead of suppressing them fiercely, based on what they had done and what they were continuing to do in all their guises, they wanted to bring them in to the VRS. And that seemed to be more important and they seemed to be acceptable as long as they were within the VRS or under the control of the Serb authorities.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah. Yes. Because they go on to list -- or he -- sorry, he goes on to list groups active in the area of Prijedor, including this group headed by, I think you've mentioned already, Cigo's Group headed by this man called Radanovic. Then we see Veljko Milankovic from Prnjavor and is recently formally under the command of the 1KK; the Serbian Defence forces, Nenad Stevandic, who's a member of the -- well, it doesn't say that here but, anyway, there is a connection between SJB and SNB. And over in the next page, please, we see that a Special Police unit, under the command of a certain Kujundzic, has been established in the village of Stanari in the municipality of Doboj and consists of about 80 men who are mainly involved in setting up check-points which they use for their criminal activities. Now, that report was the 28th of July. And I think you reference, in your report, at paragraph 2.63, that Major Talic -- sorry, General Talic issued his own instruction which we can see, please, as P593, tab 38. And the -- he refers to the assessment in the first paragraph, two days before, and then he orders: Offer all paramilitary formations and their leaders ... if they do honestly intend to serve the rightful struggle for survival of the Serbian people an opportunity -- and we need to go over to the next page, please -- to join the regular army. And then item 2: Do not include in the units individuals and groups which have been involved in crimes and looting or who have committed other criminal acts. Disarm and arrest them and bring criminal charges against them in the army courts, regardless of their citizenship. Now, this is end of July. Were there any documents earlier that you saw in relation to any dealings with paramilitaries that show any suggestion that these people should be charged with criminal offences? Or was that the first time?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're talking about General Talic issuing an instruction similar --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... yes, instruction, exactly.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that was the first time. I could be wrong. But from memory I think that was the only one I remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And then 3, again, this -- might as well look at the B/C/S word -- well, here it says, in cooperation with the SRBH MUP, disarm and arrest paramilitary formations, et cetera, et cetera. And finally, under 5: I forbid the existence of any paramilitary units, groups, and individuals, in the territory. From now on, bring criminal charges against those commanders, competent military territorial organs. Now, it says there that he forbids the existence of any paramilitary units. And I think you go on in your report, however, to point out or to give the full example of what happened to Milankovic and indeed other paramilitary groups.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I should just note, in passing, that in paragraph 2.67 it appears to read on the 23rd of December, "1992." That should read "1991." It was corrected by Mr. Brown in an addendum.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It appears that these -- this paramilitary organisation continued to exist because it was part of the Krajina Corps; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I mean, I think, at least from the documents I was able to review, I certainly know that those two, Cigo's Group, for example, and also Milankovic's Group, were -- continued to be part of the VRS and clearly were not -- well, it says "do not include individuals or groups," well, his unit continued to -- Milankovic's unit continued to operate until his death.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And indeed ... yes. All right. That's all I want to deal with on paramilitaries. Can we move, then, please, to some of the features of the municipality attacks which you start to deal with at paragraph 2.73. And I think you already indicated earlier that there was a similarity that occurred during these military attacks and operations which have been carried out, and you describe that in paragraph 2.73 and indeed 2.74. You go on to deal with the incidents as against the Serb forces, which preceded, as you put it, some of the municipality attacks. And if we look at one of the documents, dated the 1st of June, which is document at number 17, which is P411.29 -- I think we've looked at that, sorry. Yes, I've got the wrong document. No, I haven't. I asked you earlier about the reporting up of these attacks and the responsibility to taking these attacks. So if we look at this report, 1st of June, from the 1st Krajina Corps, at the bottom of the page - first page in English and second page in -- middle paragraph, second page in B/C/S, I think. The heaviest fighting has taken place -- yeah, in the area of Hambarine, Prijedor, Kozarac, troops under the command of the Prijedor area cleared Hambarine and Kozarac and completely destroyed one ZNG unit, which is apparently black shirts, foreign mercenaries, and legionaries, and the troops have arrested more than 2.000 Green Berets who are now in Omarska. 135 of them in Stara Gradiska and about 5.000 in the village of Trnopolje. What does this report demonstrate, as far as you're concerned, in the themes that you were looking at in your report?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think, again, you know, there is an involvement of the army. There's a large number of people captured as a result very quickly, and they're placed in detention centres very quickly, or at least arrested. And there was references after that of General Talic commending that operation. And, again, it would seem to be one of those quite quick operations. To take that number of people and control that number of people is not an easy logistic issue if they were all combatants.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I was going to ask about that. According to this, they have arrested 2.000 Green Berets. Does that Green Berets suggest these are supposed to be armed combatants?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: They categorise Green Berets generally as combatants. 2.000 is a lot. 5.000 people in Trnopolje is a lot of people. I'm not sure they can all be combatants. I think I find that very difficult.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah. While we are on this report, can we go to the third page, please, in English, and it's the fourth page in B/C/S. It says, at the end: This report shall be thrashed out with the soldiers -- sorry, with all soldiers. Specifying the facts that it presents more credible than those in the mass media. You spoke yesterday of dissemination of the, as it were, the plans, the underlying -- I suppose the word is ideology behind what was happening. Is this -- can this be categorised as an example of that?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think it could be certainly seen as a report that indicates that the corps wanted to ensure its soldiers knew what was going on and why. This particular type of report was written by Colonel Vukalic, who was an assistant commander for moral guidance and legal affairs. It was a position, a particular staff position, in the corps. And what this officer would do, and his role really, was to ensure that the troops knew what was happening and that subordinate formations from the corps were made aware. So he would produce usually monthly reports. Sometimes they were more frequently than that. And they were summary documents about what was -- what had happened in the period prior to that. So it's not necessarily a combat report as we've seen before which tended to be daily reports about the situation. This is more of a consorted report that he would produce every so often. And he clearly wants this to be disseminated down the corps and into -- into the units.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Finally on this report, although it's on a slightly different topic, but just so, again, we don't have to go back to it, can we go back to the first page. In the third paragraph, starting in the Banja Luka region, Colonel Vukalic then goes on to deal with, again, this question of moving out. And he says that a portion of the Muslims and -- Muslim and Croatian population is moving out, the region of Bosnian Krajina has issued a decision to facilitate such departures, providing that the Serbs from Central Bosnia and places with predominant Muslim and Croatian populations are also allowed to move out. Those departing will not be allowed to return. Would part of Colonel Vukalic's job as the morale officer, as it were, be to liaise with the civilian authorities, for example the ARK Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that that was his role. The corps did have an officer for civilian affairs which was separate to this, but clearly this is a job that requires to receive information about what's going on, and he clearly knows about this decision, and he's aware that the population is moving out and that they are not going to be allowed to return. And again, on your previous point, that this information should be disseminated down or thrashed out, as he calls it, with soldiers, clearly shows that, you know, that this is an issue that they are to be made aware of, or at least they haven't got any problems with them being made aware that that is the situation. And, again, I keep coming back to the issue of time. This is the 1st of June. This is with only weeks from the 16th Assembly Session, weeks from the formation of the army, and already there's references that large numbers of people are moving out or that there are large numbers of people in detention.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Yes, thank you. That's all I'm going to ask from that document. And if I'm looking at your paragraph 2.76, you conclude that the -- these incidents that -- against the Serb forces were low-level ones, even though they resulted in the death of Serb soldiers, and that the response to them, as you say, was often significant, both in terms of manpower and weapons system used. What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, I -- I did see in the documents that there were instances where Serbs were attacked, you know, especially in the early part of May, and there were a number of incidents -- the Hambarine check-point incident being one, where Serb soldiers and police, I believe, or military police, were attacked. There was an incident in Kljuc where a bus was attacked carrying JNA soldiers. And incidents resulted in the deaths of Serbs. But they did seem somewhat low-level in terms of casualties, and within days sometimes, within days, you had what appeared to be large-scale military operations, combined operations, sometimes involving tanks - as a reference, I think in the attack on Prijedor, that tanks were used. There are references in the 1 Krajina Corps of massive bombardment and destruction of towns and villages, and it seemed to be that the incidents were -- the unfortunate incidents where soldiers or Serbs were killed did seem somewhat low-level in comparison to what followed, the rounding up of thousands of people and the destruction of a lot of -- a lot of property, which -- some of which is referenced in the documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You've talked about the use of tanks and the like. Would the brigades that were involved in these attacks have their own tanks or heavy artillery, or would they need to request the use of those?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certain brigades of the corps would have had some tank support. I don't know the exact distribution. For example, in the motorised brigade, 43rd Brigade, it may have had its own tank support. There was a tank brigade within the corps. It's its own armoured brigade. And normally when armour is used, it's not used as a brigade on its own; it's usually given in support of other operations. So Talic probably had the option of disseminating out armour to units, and probably some units of his corps also had armour. It was a bit similar in relation to artillery, although artillery comes in many forms. And infantry and Territorial Defence units would have had things like mortars and maybe even small calibre artillery pieces. But there were larger artillery pieces in certain units of the corps. So, in essence, it's a bit of a mix.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I've reached the end of that section, so perhaps it would be an appropriate moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, as indicated to you, your testimony has a ways to go yet. And, again, as we would have indicated, the Court will not be sitting for the rest of this week in observance of the Orthodox New Years, observed according to the Julian calendar. So we would continue your testimony at 9.00. We are scheduled for, in this courtroom, on Monday morning, yes, and I trust that everyone has a safe weekend.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 17th day of January, 2011, at 9.00 a.m.
